answers: The Shroud of Turin is supposedly the burial cloth that was wrapped around Jesus after his crucifixion; bloodstains on the linen shroud, which are said to have been transferred to it during the three days Jesus was in the tomb, form the image of a crucified man. But a new study reported in the Journal of Forensic Sciences finds the bloodstain image was likely faked. Researchers looking at the blood spatter found that the stains appeared to come from someone standing up, rather than someone who was flat on the fabric, Science Alert reports. As the researchers put it, the stains are "totally unrealistic" when compared to what they should look like. The shroud, which is held in the Cathedral of St. John the Baptist in Italy, is considered an icon, as opposed to a genuine religious relic, by the Vatican; Fox News notes "the church has never weighed in on its authenticity." "This is the kind of forensic work done all the time in police investigations," the forensic scientist who conducted the analysis tells BuzzFeed News. "Even a crucified or hanging person should leave a distinct blood pattern on the cloth, which would be fascinating information to have." The study found inconsistent staining, with researchers concluding multiple poses were used to create the bloodstains—a standing model was likely used to imprint patterns on the cloth at various angles for various body parts. Another bloodstain pattern expert notes that more research could be done to see whether cleaning a body or preparing it for burial might account for the inconsistent staining, though he notes that the stains do appear to have come from flowing blood, meaning a heart that was beating at the time the stains were made. (See previous stories in the real-or-fake debate here.)

**Summary of News on the Shroud of Turin**

The Shroud of Turin, a 14-foot-long linen cloth bearing the image of a crucified man, has long been a subject of religious and scientific fascination. Revered by some Christians as the burial cloth of Jesus of Nazareth, the shroud has been the focus of numerous studies and debates over its authenticity. Recent forensic research, published in the *Journal of Forensic Sciences*, has added new evidence suggesting that the shroud may be a medieval forgery.

A team of researchers, including forensic anthropologist Matteo Borrini from Liverpool John Moores University and organic chemist Luigi Garlaschelli from the University of Pavia, conducted a detailed analysis of the bloodstain patterns on the shroud. Using real and synthetic blood, they tested various positions and movements to replicate the blood flow patterns seen on the cloth. Their findings indicate that the bloodstains are inconsistent with any single pose, such as a crucified or supine body.

For instance, the blood flow on the forearm and hand suggests different angles of movement, which are not compatible with a single position. The researchers found that the bloodstains on the hand and forearm would only occur if the arms were held at specific angles—some at 45 degrees, others at 90 degrees—contradicting the idea of a crucified or lying-down body. Additionally, the blood pattern around the spear wound and the lower back could not be replicated in any tested position, further supporting the theory that the shroud was not made from a real crucified body.

The study also noted that the bloodstains on the shroud do not align with the expected patterns from a crucified individual, suggesting that the image may have been created using a standing model. This conclusion adds to the growing body of evidence that the shroud is a medieval artistic or didactic representation rather than an authentic relic from the time of Jesus.

Despite these findings, the shroud remains a subject of intrigue. Radiocarbon dating from 1988 placed the shroud between 1260 and 1390 CE, which aligns with the Middle Ages, not the time of Jesus. While the origin of the image on the cloth remains a mystery, the latest forensic analysis has provided compelling evidence that challenges the authenticity of the shroud. The Vatican has never officially confirmed or denied its authenticity, treating it as an icon rather than a religious relic.

The research highlights the ongoing scientific interest
